chapter: Los Angeles with Mutt Carey and the taxi dances
title: Banjos replacing guitars; 12th and Central and the Hummingbird
summary: New Orleans musicians in Los Angeles gathered at 12th and Central, the Hummingbird nightclub and two New Orleans restaurants.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: The early New Orleans bands or bands from the South had guitar. But by this time it seems to me like the guitars had been replaced by banjos.

That's right. I think Frank would bring his guitar once in a while, when it wasn't in hock. Which it's true, a lot of times I'd just be playing my alto saxophone because my soprano would be in hock, you see. But I never hocked my alto, because I had to have it.
The New Orleans musicians in that particular band, there was Ram and George Foster, you...well, practically everybody except Alex Hill.
Did they kind of stick together in a group, or did they...was everybody together?

Not really. But at that time, they had quite a few New Orleans musicians in Los Angeles. And when we'd all congregate here... If you wanted to find any musician in Los Angeles, you could go to 12th and Central, which is the slums now. But 12th and Central was the hangout for all of the musicians. And they had a prominent nightclub, where some of your top entertainers, like Bojangles Bill Robinson played -- it was called the Hummingbird. Of course, Bojangles played the Orpheum circuit. He was one of the first Black guys that played on

a big circuit like the Orpheum, or the Pantages.
They had two New Orleans restaurants. One reason why
these musicians...the New Orleans musicians... The Maybelle
and the New Orleans Kitchen, I believe, or the New Orleans
Panty. You could go get red beans and rice and whatever you
wanted, get gumbo there all the time.
